lessons.t: Team shapes: smaller pods, PMs who build, engineers who spec
lessons.html:
Chapter 8, AI coding, now and next, showed that a coding agent can take a clear spec to a working prototype in a day. That changes the economics of a product team. When building is cheap, the scarce resources become deciding what to build, defining what good looks like, and reviewing what got built. Team shape should follow the scarce resources.

What moves

  • PMs build. A PM who can prototype with an agent settles a debate in an afternoon with a working thing users can try. The prototype is evidence for a decision. It is never the production system, and the PM who built it should say so loudly.
  • Engineers spec. The spec is now the agent’s input, so the engineer who writes a precise spec, with an eval attached, gets more leverage than the one who types fastest. Engineers also write a large share of the eval cases for tool calls and structured outputs, because they know where the edges are.
  • Designers ship. Anthropic has described its product designers feeding Figma files to Claude Code and iterating on working code, with people reviewing the result (July 2025). Expect designers to own more of the interaction layer directly.
  • Domain experts join the pod. The person who can tell a good answer from a plausible one is part of the core team. In legal, medical, finance or support products this is often the most important hire you make.
DimensionClassic squadAI-native pod
Size6–9 engineers plus PM and designerSmaller: often 2–4 engineers, PM, designer, part-time domain expert (illustrative)
BottleneckEngineering capacityReview, evals and decisions
RequirementsPRD with user storiesSpec with an eval set and pass thresholds (Chapter 5)
Definition of doneTests pass, design QA signed offTests pass and eval gates pass, with a trace review
Shared servicesDesign system, CI, data platformAlso a model gateway, eval harness, tracing and an approved-model list

The platform layer

Small pods only work if they don’t each rebuild the same plumbing. Somebody has to own the model gateway (routing, keys, rate limits, cost attribution), the tracing stack (Chapter 10, Reliability and observability), the eval harness, the prompt and context registry, and the security controls from Chapter 12. Put that in one platform team with a clear service contract. Without it, five pods ship five tracing formats and nobody can compare quality or cost across features.

The trap

Smaller pods produce more code per person, and that code still needs review. If you cut headcount in proportion to output gains, review becomes the queue everything waits in. Size pods by review and eval capacity, then let agents fill the gap in typing.

Two shapes to avoid

  • The central AI team that builds models or prompts and hands them to product teams. It separates the people who define quality from the people who see users, and it becomes a queue.
  • Every pod for itself, with no shared eval tooling or cost attribution. You lose the ability to say which features are profitable or improving.

What changes for you

  • Staff pods by review and eval capacity. Ask “who reviews this, and who reads the traces?” before “who builds this?”
  • Name a domain expert in every AI pod, with protected hours, and treat it as a staffing requirement.
  • Prototype the riskiest interaction yourself before writing the spec, and label the prototype as throwaway.
  • Push for a platform team that owns the gateway, tracing and eval harness, so pods spend their time on product quality.

lessons.t: Who owns evals, context and model choice
lessons.html:
AI features fail in the gaps between roles. The prompt that nobody owns gets edited in production by whoever is on call. The eval set that belongs to everyone stops getting new cases after launch. The model upgrade that sits between platform and product slips until a deprecation notice forces it. Fix this with explicit ownership, decided before launch and written into the spec.

The principle

The person accountable for what “good” means owns the eval content. For most features that is the PM, or a domain expert the PM delegates to. Hamel Husain’s evals FAQ recommends that smaller teams appoint a single domain expert as the final judge of quality, with inter-annotator agreement measured once several people label. Engineering owns the machinery that runs the evals and keeps the LLM judge calibrated. Context and model choice sit with whoever can be held to the quality and cost numbers at the same time.

Decision or artefactAccountableResponsibleMust be consulted
Eval set content and rubricPMDomain expert, PMEngineering, support
Eval harness and LLM-judge calibrationEng leadEngineers, platformPM
Pass thresholds and launch gatesPMPM, eng leadSecurity, design
Context spec and system promptPMEngineers, PMDomain expert
Tool descriptions and schemasEng leadEngineersPM
Model choice per taskPMEngineers run the bake-offPlatform, finance
Approved-model list and vendor termsPlatform leadPlatformSecurity, legal
Model upgrade go or no-goPMEng lead runs shadow and evalsPlatform, support
Cost budget per userPMEngineersFinance
Launch risk reviewSecurity leadPM prepares itLegal, privacy

Treat the table as a starting point. What matters is that each row has exactly one accountable name, written down.

Prompts and context are code

A system prompt change can move quality more than a week of feature work, and it can break a feature as thoroughly as a bad deploy. So context changes go through version control, code review and the same eval gate as code (Chapter 5, Evals are the spec, on regression gates). The PM approves changes to behaviour. Engineering approves changes to structure, such as cache layout, token budget and tool wiring (Chapter 4, Context engineering).

Model choice is a product decision

Picking a model trades quality, latency and cost at once, and those are product trade-offs. Engineering runs the bake-off from Chapter 3, Reading the frontier. The PM decides, with the eval scores, latency percentiles and cost per task in front of them. Platform constrains the choice to models that have passed security and contract review.

The orphan test

Pick any AI feature in production. Ask three people who would approve a change to its system prompt, who added the last eval case, and who decides when to move it to a new model. If you get different answers, you have found your next incident.

What changes for you

  • Add an ownership table to every AI spec, with one accountable name per row.
  • Require every prompt or context change to cite an eval run, the same way code changes cite tests.
  • Own model choice explicitly. If engineering is choosing models alone, they are also making your margin and quality decisions alone.

lessons.t: Rituals: trace reviews, eval reviews, model upgrade days
lessons.html:
A team that ships probabilistic software needs habits that make quality visible every week. Code review and sprint demos aren’t enough, because a feature can pass every unit test and still get worse. The rituals below are the minimum set. Each produces a decision or a change to the eval set. A ritual that only produces discussion should be cut.

RitualCadenceWhoInputOutput
Trace reviewWeekly, 45 minutesPM, domain expert, one engineer20–50 sampled traces, weighted toward failures and low ratingsNew failure categories, new eval cases, one fix to try
Eval reviewEvery two weeks, 30 minutesPod plus platform repEval trend by category, pass^k on critical cases, judge agreementThreshold changes, coverage gaps, next quality bet
Model upgrade dayWhen a candidate model ships or a deprecation landsEng lead, PM, platformShadow run, full eval, cost and latency diffGo, no-go or route-only decision, with a rollout plan
Cost reviewMonthlyPM, eng lead, financeCost per user at median and p95, cache hit rate, top spendersRouting or caching changes, price or limit changes
AI incident reviewAfter every incidentWhoever was involvedTraces of the failing sessionsEval cases that would have caught it, guardrail changes

Trace review

This is error analysis from Chapter 5 turned into a habit. Read whole traces: the context the model saw, each tool call, the output and what the user did next. Tag failures with open notes first, then cluster them. Most teams find that a handful of categories cover most failures, which gives the roadmap a priority order for free. Rotate the engineer each week so everyone keeps a feel for real behaviour.

Eval review

Look at the trend, then the failures behind any movement. The standing questions: which categories moved, did the judge still agree with humans on the spot-checked sample, which production failures from trace review have become eval cases, and is any case so easy that it no longer tells you anything. The eval set should grow every fortnight. One that stopped growing at launch is measuring the product you had then.

Model upgrade day

Schedule it the way you would schedule a dependency upgrade with a security deadline. Vendors retire models on published timelines. As of October 2026 Anthropic, for example, commits to at least 60 days’ notice before retiring a publicly released model, which is less time than a quarterly planning cycle. Run the playbook from Chapter 10: shadow traffic, full eval, cost and latency comparison, prompt adjustments, staged rollout. Doing it on a fixed day keeps upgrades routine instead of urgent.

Replace deadline demos

Hamel Husain’s field guide argues for time-boxed experiments with decision points over feature deadlines, because nobody can promise that a capability will reach a quality bar by a date. Keep demos, but make every demo show its eval number next to the happy path.

What changes for you

  • Put a weekly trace review in your own calendar and attend it. It is the cheapest way to stay calibrated on what the product actually does.
  • Measure ritual health by outputs: eval cases added per fortnight, failure categories closed, upgrades shipped before deadline.
  • Write roadmap items for uncertain capabilities as experiments with a decision date and a threshold, then report them in the eval review.

lessons.t: Hiring and leveling for AI product roles
lessons.html:
The AI PM job description has changed faster than most leveling guides. Hiring panels still test roadmap prioritisation and stakeholder management, which matter, and skip the skills that separate AI PMs who ship from those who demo. Interview for judgement under uncertainty, measured with real outputs.

What to test, and how

SkillInterview exerciseStrong signalRed flag
Error analysisGive 30 real, anonymised outputs from a feature. Ask for a failure taxonomy in 25 minutes.Reads every output, builds categories from the data, counts them, picks the one to fix firstJumps to “use a better model” or proposes a metric before reading
Eval designTurn a vague requirement into an eval: cases, rubric, threshold.Covers the long tail, separates capability from reliability, sets a pass rateWrites prose acceptance criteria or a single example
Cost reasoningEstimate cost per user per month for a described feature.Gets within an order of magnitude, names session length and caching as leversCan’t estimate tokens, ignores heavy users
Autonomy judgementPick an autonomy level for an agent that edits customer records.Ties the level to error cost, reversibility and the eval numberPicks full autonomy because the demo worked
BuildingWalk through something they built with an agent.Can say what broke, what they threw away and what review costOnly screenshots; no sense of what hardening means

Leveling

Use your existing ladder and add AI-specific expectations at each level. A reasonable shape:

  • PM. Owns the eval set for one feature and runs its trace review. Writes context specs that engineering can implement without a meeting.
  • Senior PM. Owns quality, cost and model choice for a product area. Has taken at least one feature through a model upgrade. Can defend a margin.
  • Staff or principal PM. Sets eval and launch standards across teams, shapes the platform roadmap, and owns the bets and kill criteria from Chapter 13, Strategy on a moving frontier.

The rest of the team

The authors of What We’ve Learned From A Year of Building with LLMs recommend staging hiring: build the product first (AI engineers help, but aren’t strictly required), then instrument and collect data, then bring in ML engineers to optimise evals, retrieval and experiments. Hiring an ML team before you have traffic and traces tends to produce infrastructure with nothing to measure. They also stress that a domain expert is always needed, often the PM at larger companies.

Upskill first

Your strongest existing PMs already know the users, the data and the politics. Most of the AI-specific skills in the table above can be taught in a quarter with labs like the ones in this course. Hire externally for depth you can’t grow in time, such as eval engineering or applied ML. In the EU, the AI Act’s AI literacy article has applied to providers and deployers since 2 February 2025, so structured training also has a compliance angle.

What changes for you

  • Add an error-analysis exercise with real outputs to every AI PM loop. It predicts on-the-job performance better than a product sense case.
  • Rewrite your leveling guide so eval ownership, cost ownership and model upgrades appear at named levels.
  • Sequence hires to the product’s stage. No ML team before you have traces worth optimising.

lessons.t: Capstone: the complete AI feature spec
lessons.html:
Every chapter in this course ended with one artefact. A real AI feature needs all of them, and they constrain each other. The autonomy level from Chapter 6 sets the risk review in Chapter 12, which sets the guardrails in the runbook from Chapter 10. The eval threshold from Chapter 5 decides which model from Chapter 3 is good enough, which sets the cost model from Chapter 1, which sets the price in Chapter 11. Change one and others move. The capstone spec is the place those dependencies are made explicit and checked.

Why one document

Separate artefacts drift. The pricing brief assumes a small model; the eval spec was passed on a frontier model; the risk review approved a draft-only agent that has since been given write access. Each document is internally sound, and the feature as a whole is wrong. A single spec with cross-references forces the contradictions into view before launch.

If you changeRe-checkBecause
Model or tier (Ch 3)Eval results, cost model, runbook, risk reviewQuality, cost and safety behaviour all shift with the model
Autonomy level (Ch 6)Interaction spec, risk review, eval thresholdsHigher autonomy raises error cost and needs higher pass^k
Knowledge architecture (Ch 7)Context spec, permissions, latency budgetRetrieval changes what the model sees and who can see what
Eval threshold (Ch 5)Model choice, launch date, kill criteriaA higher bar may need a bigger model or more time
Pricing (Ch 11)Usage limits, heavy-user cost, routingPrice sets how much cost per user you can carry
Tools or data access (Ch 6, 12)Threat model, permissions, runbookNew access can complete the lethal trifecta

The panel

The capstone is reviewed by a panel from product, engineering and security, ideally with finance or a domain expert on call. Send the spec 48 hours ahead. In the session, the author gets five minutes to state the bet. The rest is questions against the rubric in the lab. The panel scores each criterion and the spec passes only if no criterion scores 1 and the risk and eval criteria both score 3. Failing is a normal outcome. A spec that fails with clear actions has done its job.

What good looks like

  • Every number has a source: an eval run, a bake-off, a trace sample or a labelled illustrative estimate.
  • The kill criteria are measurable and dated, and someone has agreed to act on them.
  • The spec says what would make it obsolete, such as a model six months out doing the task natively (Chapter 13).
  • It is short. Aim for something a reviewer can read in 30 minutes, with links to the full eval set and traces.

Use it as your team’s template

Once your capstone passes, strip the content out and keep the structure. The sections, the dependency table and the rubric make a better AI PRD template than most teams have.

What changes for you

  • Write AI specs as one document with cross-references, so a change in one section flags the others.
  • Hold a panel review for any AI feature that acts on user data or carries a margin risk, and record the scores.
  • Re-run the dependency table whenever the model, autonomy level or pricing changes.

lab.title: Capstone: take one AI feature from idea to a reviewed spec
lab.time: about 4 hours of writing, plus a 60-minute panel review
lab.intro: This lab is the course’s finale. You will take one AI feature from idea to a complete spec that uses every earlier chapter, check that its sections agree with each other, and defend it in front of a panel from product, engineering and security.
steps: Pick the feature. Choose a real feature you could ship in the next two quarters, on one surface, that makes at least one model call and uses either retrieval or a tool. Write section 0 in under 150 words: the user problem, the metric that moves, its baseline and a target date.

Gather your artefacts. Collect what you produced in Chapters 1–13: the cost model, failure memo, model selection memo, context spec, eval spec, agent design doc, knowledge decision record, team playbook, interaction spec, runbook, pricing brief, risk review and strategy page. Mark each as reusable, needs updating for this feature, or missing.

Write the foundation sections (1–7). Fill sections 1–7 of the template for this feature. Every number needs a source: an eval run, a bake-off, a trace sample or an estimate labelled illustrative. The eval spec needs at least 50 cases, a written rubric and both a pass threshold and a pass^k threshold for critical cases.

Write the shipping sections (8–14). Fill sections 8–14. Give the margin at both median and p95 usage under your chosen price. Run at least ten injection attempts against the design if it reads untrusted content. Make kill criteria measurable and dated, and name who acts on them.

Check coherence. Walk the dependency table from lesson 5 row by row. For each pair, confirm the sections agree: the model in section 3 is the one the eval in section 5 passed on and the one priced in section 11; the autonomy level in section 6 is the one the risk review in section 12 approved. Fix every contradiction you find.

Run a pre-mortem. Assume it is six months after launch and the feature has been killed. Write the three most likely reasons in one paragraph each. Make sure each one is caught by an eval case, a monitor in the runbook or a kill criterion. Add whatever is missing.

Hold the panel. Send the spec to a panel of at least three people from product, engineering and security 48 hours ahead. In 60 minutes, present the bet for five minutes, then take questions. Each panellist scores the rubric independently before discussion, then agree final scores.

Revise and schedule. Address every criterion that scored below 3, record the scores and actions in the spec, and set a re-review trigger: the next model upgrade day, a change of autonomy level or the first kill-criteria checkpoint, whichever comes first.
lab.template:
Capstone spec template

#SectionFrom chapterThe question it must answerEvidence expected

Panel review rubric

Criterion1: Not ready2: Needs work3: Ready
Problem and betNo measurable outcomeOutcome named, no baseline or dateBaseline, target and date, tied to a strategy bet
Eval rigourProse criteria or a handful of examplesGolden set exists but thin on the long tail or judge uncalibratedCoverage of the long tail, calibrated judge, pass^k on critical cases, threshold justified
Model and contextModel chosen by reputationBake-off run, context spec looseBake-off on own tasks, context budget and cache layout specified, re-evaluation trigger set
Autonomy and UX fitAutonomy level missing or unjustifiedLevel set, failure UX partialLevel tied to error cost and eval results, three failure paths designed
EconomicsNo cost estimateMedian cost onlyMedian and p95 cost, margin under the chosen price, levers identified
RiskNo threat modelThreat model without testingThreat model, injection tests run, permissions minimal, sign-off owner named
OperabilityNo tracing or rollback planTracing planned, no upgrade pathSLOs, tracing, rollback and model upgrade playbook rehearsed
CoherenceSections contradict each otherMinor inconsistenciesDependency table checked; every number has a source

Pass rule: no criterion scores 1, and both Eval rigour and Risk score 3. Record scores and actions in the spec.
lab.done: A spec of roughly ten to fifteen pages with all fifteen sections filled, every number sourced, no contradictions left in the dependency table, and a recorded panel score that meets the pass rule. Your team could start building from it on Monday, and a new PM could run the feature from it in a month.

quiz.q: Your org cuts a pod from eight engineers to three after coding agents roughly double output per engineer. Two months later, merged PRs are flat and the review queue is a week long. What should you change first?
o: Add more coding agent licences so the three engineers produce more
Size the pod around review and eval capacity, adding reviewers or reducing work in progress
Let the agents merge their own PRs when CI passes
Move the PM to writing code full-time
quiz.w: The constraint moved from typing to review. Adding output into a saturated review queue makes the queue longer, so capacity and work in progress need to match review throughput.

quiz.q: A production system prompt was changed by the on-call engineer to stop a bad answer. Quality on two other categories dropped and nobody noticed for three weeks. What is the root-cause fix?
o: Ban engineers from editing prompts
Move prompts into the model’s weights via fine-tuning
Treat context as code: version control, a named accountable owner and an eval gate on every change
Add a daily manual spot-check of five answers
quiz.w: The failure is an unowned, ungated artefact. Versioning, ownership and a regression gate catch cross-category damage before it ships.

quiz.q: Engineering picked a model for a new feature because it led a public leaderboard. Who should decide model choice, and on what basis?
o: The platform team, from the leaderboard
The vendor’s solutions engineer
Engineering, because it is a technical decision
The PM, from a bake-off on the team’s own tasks covering quality, latency and cost, within the platform’s approved list
quiz.w: Model choice trades quality, latency and margin at once, which are product decisions. Engineering runs the bake-off; platform constrains the options.

quiz.q: Your team’s eval set has had no new cases since launch six months ago, and scores are steady at 94%. What is the most likely reading?
o: The eval is measuring the product you had at launch, and new production failures aren’t in it
The feature is stable and the eval is working
The LLM judge has drifted upward
The model has improved and you should raise the threshold
quiz.w: Trace and incident reviews should feed new cases every fortnight. A static set keeps passing while real failure modes go unmeasured.

quiz.q: You are hiring a senior AI PM. Which exercise best predicts whether they will improve a live AI feature?
o: A product sense case about a new market
Thirty real outputs from a feature, with 25 minutes to build a failure taxonomy and choose what to fix first
A whiteboard explanation of transformer attention
A take-home PRD for a non-AI feature
quiz.w: Error analysis from real outputs is the core habit of AI product work, and it exposes whether a candidate reads data before reaching for a fix.

quiz.q: During the capstone panel, security notices the agent now has write access to CRM records, but the risk review approved a draft-only design. What should happen?
o: Approve the spec, since the eval scores are high
Lower the eval threshold to compensate
Score Coherence and Risk below 3, and re-run the risk review, interaction spec and eval thresholds for the new autonomy level
Ask the vendor whether write access is safe
quiz.w: A change in autonomy level invalidates the downstream sections. The dependency table exists to catch exactly this, and the pass rule requires Risk to score 3.

deliverable.title: The capstone spec, panel-reviewed
deliverable.html:
A single document for one AI feature, built from the capstone template and signed off by a panel from product, engineering and security. Put a one-page cover sheet on top so a busy reviewer can decide in five minutes:

  1. The bet. The user problem, the metric, its baseline and the target date, in three sentences.
  2. The design in one table. Model and tier per task, autonomy level, knowledge architecture, and the context budget.
  3. The quality bar. Eval size, launch threshold, pass^k on critical cases and current score.
  4. The economics. Cost per user at median and p95, price, and gross margin at both.
  5. The top three risks with their controls and the named sign-off owner.
  6. Kill criteria and re-review triggers, each measurable and dated.
  7. Ownership and rituals. One accountable name per decision, and the dates of the first trace review, eval review and model upgrade day.
  8. Panel scores against the rubric, with open actions.

Behind the cover sheet sit the fifteen sections, with links to the eval set, traces and bake-off data. When it passes, strip out the content and offer the structure to your team as its AI spec template.
